question.text: Given the diagram shown above, what is the measure of $\overline{BC}?$
question.explanation:
The segments addition postulate can be applied to a set of more than three collinear points. In the given situation, it states that \[ AD = AB + BC +CD. \]

Substituting the known values into the equation above, we obtain:

\begin{align} AD& = AB + BC +CD \\[3pt] 28 & = 9+BC+7 \\[3pt] 28 & = 16+BC \\[3pt] 28-16 & = BC \\[3pt] BC & = 12 \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Distance Between More Than Three Collinear Points

question.text: Given the diagram shown above, what is the value of $x?$
question.explanation:
By the segment addition postulate, we have \[ AD = AB + BC +CD. \]

To solve for $x,$ we can substitute the given information

\[ AD=49, \quad AB=2x+1, \quad BC=3x, \quad CD=8, \]

and then solve the resulting equation:

\begin{align} AD& = AB + BC +CD \\[3pt] 49 & = (2x+1)+3x+8 \\[3pt] 49 & = 5x+9 \\[3pt] 5x & = 40 \\[3pt] x & = 8 \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Value of an Unknown Quantity Using Collinearity

question.text: Given the diagram shown above, what is the value of $x?$
question.explanation:
By the segment addition postulate, we have \[ AD = AB + BC +CD. \]

To solve for $x,$ we can substitute the given information

\[ AD=11, \quad AB=2x+3, \quad BC=1-6x, \quad CD=3, \]

and then solve the resulting equation:

\begin{align} AD& = AB + BC +CD \\[3pt] 11 & = (2x+3)+(1-6x)+3 \\[3pt] 11 & = -4x+7 \\[3pt] 4x & = -4 \\[3pt] x & = -1 \end{align}
